title: PostgreSQL HA with Patroni, etcd, HAProxy and Mattermost

release.label: Enrolled learner release — clean baseline verified

phases.title: Learn the system one idea at a time

steps.title: Why high availability exists
steps.why: A business application should not lose its database service because one database server stops.
steps.scenario: Mattermost is used during a workday when its database server suddenly fails.
steps.definition: High availability is a system's ability to keep providing its required service when an expected component fails.
plain_parts: The required service here is safe database reads and writes.
Expected failures are handled by another prepared component.
steps.example: A prepared replica becomes the writer after the primary fails.
steps.benefit: Planned redundancy can reduce application downtime.
steps.limitation: High availability does not prevent every outage or replace backups.

visual.alt: Mattermost first depends on one database, then continues through a replacement writer after that database fails.

steps.checkpoint: In one sentence, what service must remain available when a database server fails?

steps.title: Meet the eight stable roles
steps.why: Names based on responsibilities remain understandable even when cloud addresses change.
steps.scenario: A platform team hands a DBA eight clean servers identified by workplace roles.
steps.definition: A role is the responsibility assigned to a server in the system.
plain_parts: Three dcs roles hold shared coordination state.
Three pg roles run PostgreSQL and Patroni; one router and one application role complete the request path.
steps.example: pg-ha-1 identifies a database role without depending on its current IP address.
steps.benefit: Stable roles make procedures and evidence repeatable.
steps.limitation: A role name does not prove that its service is healthy.

visual.alt: Eight boxes grouped into three DCS roles, three PostgreSQL roles, one HAProxy router and one Mattermost application.

steps.checkpoint: Name the four groups of roles and the job performed by each group.

steps.title: Separate a failure from an outage
steps.why: Operators must know whether a broken component actually removed the user-facing service.
steps.scenario: One replica is down, but Mattermost users can still post messages.
steps.definition: A failure is a component that stops working; an outage is loss of the required service.
plain_parts: A redundant component can fail without causing an outage.
Several failures or one unprotected dependency can still cause an outage.
steps.example: A replica failure reduces protection but the current primary may continue serving writes.
steps.benefit: The distinction helps an operator prioritize impact and recovery.
steps.limitation: No visible outage does not mean the system is safe to leave degraded.

visual.alt: One side shows a failed replica with service continuing; the other shows the writer path unavailable to Mattermost.

steps.checkpoint: Why must a DBA repair a failed replica even when users see no outage?

steps.title: What the distributed configuration store does
steps.why: Several Patroni nodes need one shared place to coordinate who may lead.
steps.scenario: Three database nodes must agree which one is allowed to accept writes.
steps.definition: A distributed configuration store is a service that keeps small pieces of shared coordination state consistently across several members.
plain_parts: Distributed means several members cooperate.
Coordination state records facts such as the current leader lock; it is not application table data.
steps.example: etcd stores Patroni's current leader key.
steps.benefit: Nodes make leadership decisions from shared consensus-backed state.
steps.limitation: The DCS does not copy PostgreSQL rows or replace database backups.

visual.alt: Three Patroni nodes consult one logical DCS formed by three etcd members.

steps.checkpoint: What does the DCS store for Patroni, and what does it not store?

steps.title: How quorum protects agreement
steps.why: A minority must not invent a new truth when it cannot contact most members.
steps.scenario: One of three etcd members becomes unreachable during a network problem.
steps.definition: Quorum is the minimum majority of voting members required to approve a change.
plain_parts: A majority of three is two.
One remaining member cannot safely approve new coordination state alone.
steps.example: Two reachable members can commit a leader-lock update after the third fails.
steps.benefit: Quorum prevents separated minorities from independently changing shared truth.
steps.limitation: Three members tolerate only one unavailable voting member.

visual.alt: Two of three etcd votes form quorum while one of three does not.

steps.checkpoint: How many votes form quorum in a three-member cluster, and how many failures can it tolerate?

steps.title: How Patroni earns leadership
steps.why: Only one healthy database node should hold permission to act as writer.
steps.scenario: The current writer must regularly prove it can still coordinate with the DCS.
steps.definition: A leader lease is time-limited coordination state that grants one Patroni member leadership while it continues renewing the lease.
plain_parts: Only one member owns the leader lease at a time.
The lease expires if it is not renewed, allowing a safe election under configured rules.
steps.example: A Patroni primary renews its leader lease during each healthy control loop.
steps.benefit: Time-limited ownership prevents abandoned leadership from lasting forever.
steps.limitation: Lease settings involve detection-speed and stability trade-offs.

visual.alt: A Patroni member acquires, renews and may lose a time-limited leader lease.

steps.checkpoint: Why is Patroni leadership represented by a renewable lease instead of a permanent flag?

steps.title: How PostgreSQL copies changes
steps.why: A replacement writer needs a recent copy of database changes.
steps.scenario: Mattermost commits a message on the primary while two replicas follow it.
steps.definition: Write-ahead log, or WAL, is PostgreSQL's ordered record of changes written before changed data pages; streaming replication sends WAL records from a primary to replicas.
plain_parts: The primary accepts writes and generates WAL.
Replicas receive and replay WAL to reproduce the changes.
steps.example: A committed Mattermost insert produces WAL that both replicas replay.
steps.benefit: A current replica can become a replacement primary.
steps.limitation: Replication is not a substitute for an independent backup.

visual.alt: One PostgreSQL primary sends an ordered WAL stream to two replicas that replay it.

steps.checkpoint: Trace one committed change from the primary to a replica using the term WAL.

steps.title: Choose asynchronous or synchronous replication
steps.why: A business must decide how much commit latency it will trade for stronger failure durability.
steps.scenario: The primary acknowledges a Mattermost message just before its host is lost.
steps.definition: Asynchronous replication may acknowledge a commit before a replica confirms it; synchronous replication waits for the configured replica acknowledgment before acknowledging the commit.
plain_parts: Asynchronous commits usually wait less but can leave the newest WAL only on the failed primary.
Synchronous commits wait longer but can strengthen the promise for acknowledged writes.
steps.example: A synchronous policy waits for one eligible replica before confirming a Mattermost write.
steps.benefit: The policy makes the durability-versus-latency choice explicit.
steps.limitation: A strict synchronous policy can block writes when no eligible synchronous replica exists.

visual.alt: Asynchronous commit returns before replica acknowledgment; synchronous commit waits for one replica acknowledgment.

steps.checkpoint: What trade-off changes when the cluster moves from asynchronous to synchronous replication?

steps.title: What Patroni manages
steps.why: Automation is safe only when the learner knows its responsibility and limits.
steps.scenario: A PostgreSQL primary fails and the remaining nodes need a coordinated replacement.
steps.definition: Patroni is a PostgreSQL high-availability manager that uses a DCS to coordinate leadership, configure PostgreSQL and manage promotion and replica membership.
plain_parts: Patroni observes PostgreSQL and DCS state in a repeated control loop.
It promotes or demotes nodes according to cluster state and configured safety rules.
steps.example: Patroni promotes an eligible replica after the former leader lease is no longer valid.
steps.limitation: Patroni cannot provide safe coordination without appropriate DCS access and configuration.

visual.alt: Patroni repeatedly observes PostgreSQL and etcd state, decides the safe role and applies that role locally.

steps.checkpoint: What decisions does Patroni coordinate, and which shared service does it depend on?

steps.title: How Patroni reports role health
steps.why: A router must distinguish a healthy primary from a healthy replica.
steps.scenario: All three PostgreSQL ports accept TCP connections, but only one node may receive writes.
steps.definition: Patroni's REST application programming interface exposes health endpoints whose response depends on the member's current role and state.
plain_parts: REST is an HTTP interface used here for health questions.
The primary endpoint succeeds only on the node Patroni currently considers primary under its rules.
steps.example: GET /primary returns success on the current primary and not on a replica.
steps.benefit: External routing can follow Patroni's role decision.
steps.limitation: A health response proves only the endpoint's defined condition, not whole-application health.

visual.alt: The same primary health request succeeds on one Patroni node and fails on two replica nodes.

steps.checkpoint: Why is an open PostgreSQL port weaker evidence than Patroni's primary health endpoint?

steps.title: How HAProxy finds the writer
steps.why: Applications need one stable address even when the PostgreSQL primary changes.
steps.scenario: A switchover moves the primary role from pg-ha-1 to pg-ha-2 while Mattermost keeps the same database address.
steps.definition: HAProxy is a proxy that accepts a client connection and selects an eligible backend using configured health checks.
plain_parts: The frontend is the stable address used by Mattermost.
The backend list contains PostgreSQL nodes, but only the node passing the primary check is writer-eligible.
steps.example: HAProxy routes port 5432 to the only backend whose Patroni /primary check succeeds.
steps.benefit: The application configuration does not change during a database role change.
steps.limitation: One HAProxy node remains a single point of failure in this lab profile.

visual.alt: Mattermost connects to one HAProxy frontend, which routes only to the PostgreSQL node passing the primary health check.

steps.checkpoint: What stays stable during a switchover, and what changes behind HAProxy?

steps.title: Trace the real application request
steps.why: Database process health is not enough; the user-facing workload must succeed through every dependency.
steps.scenario: A learner posts a message in Mattermost and expects it to remain readable after a database role change.
steps.definition: An application path is the complete chain of components required to serve one user action.
plain_parts: Mattermost accepts the user request and sends a database transaction to HAProxy.
HAProxy selects the primary; PostgreSQL commits the change and replication protects it according to policy.
steps.example: Post message → Mattermost → HAProxy → PostgreSQL primary → WAL replicas.
steps.benefit: Testing the whole path detects failures hidden by component-only checks.
steps.limitation: A successful database check cannot prove that Mattermost itself is available.

visual.alt: A message travels from the user to Mattermost, through HAProxy to the PostgreSQL primary, then as WAL to replicas.

steps.checkpoint: Trace a posted message through every component in order.

steps.title: State the honest HA boundary
steps.why: Engineers must not promise availability the tested architecture cannot deliver.
steps.scenario: The PostgreSQL primary fails safely, but the single HAProxy host then stops.
steps.definition: An availability boundary states which service and failure set a design is proven to tolerate.
plain_parts: This lab protects the PostgreSQL writer against selected database-node failures.
Its single HAProxy and Mattermost nodes remain unprotected application-path dependencies.
steps.example: Database HA can remain healthy while Mattermost is unavailable because HAProxy is down.
steps.benefit: An explicit boundary creates honest operational and business expectations.
steps.limitation: The lab cannot claim whole-application high availability.

visual.alt: A highlighted PostgreSQL HA boundary sits behind single HAProxy and Mattermost nodes marked as unprotected.

steps.checkpoint: Which part of this lab is highly available, and which two roles remain single points of failure?

steps.title: Why the build order matters
steps.why: A later service cannot be validated before the services it depends on exist.
steps.scenario: A DBA receives eight clean servers and must build the system without racing bootstrap or hiding failures.
steps.definition: A dependency order arranges work so each component's required inputs are ready before that component starts.
plain_parts: etcd coordination is established before Patroni needs it.
PostgreSQL and Patroni become healthy before HAProxy routes to them; Mattermost comes last as the workload proof.
steps.example: Build etcd → prepare PostgreSQL → bootstrap Patroni → configure HAProxy → connect Mattermost.
steps.benefit: Failures are isolated to the smallest unfinished layer.
steps.limitation: Starting every service at once can create ambiguous bootstrap and diagnosis problems.

visual.alt: A top-to-bottom flow shows etcd before PostgreSQL and Patroni, then HAProxy, then Mattermost.

steps.checkpoint: Put the five components in build order and explain one dependency between each adjacent pair.

steps.title: Verify the staged etcd archive
steps.why: You must prove the software bytes are approved before installing them.
steps.command_explanation: sha256sum calculates the archive fingerprint; compare it with the digest shown in the handoff manifest.
steps.expected: One SHA-256 digest followed by the archive path.
steps.hint: The digest must match character for character.

hints.question: Which value proves the staged bytes are the approved bytes?
hints.hint: Look at the first field in the output.
hints.stronger_hint: Compare it with /opt/suta/artifacts/SHA256SUMS.
hints.solution: Run sha256sum on the staged archive and stop if the digest differs.

steps.title: Install the etcd server program
steps.why: The etcd program runs one voting member of the distributed configuration store.
steps.command_explanation: sudo grants installation permission; install copies the verified server program and sets executable mode 0755.
steps.expected: The command returns to the prompt without an error and /usr/local/bin/etcd is executable.
steps.hint: The source is staged read-only; the destination is the normal local executable path.

hints.question: Which program runs the voting member service?
hints.hint: Its filename is simply etcd.
hints.stronger_hint: Use mode 0755 and destination /usr/local/bin/etcd.
hints.solution: Run the displayed install command, then wait for ETCD_SERVER_INSTALLED.

steps.title: Install the etcdctl client program
steps.why: etcdctl sends authenticated health, membership and snapshot requests to etcd.
steps.command_explanation: install copies the separately staged client program and makes it executable without starting a service.
steps.expected: The command returns to the prompt and /usr/local/bin/etcdctl is executable.
steps.hint: The source and destination names are both etcdctl.

hints.question: Which program will you use to ask the cluster for health?
hints.hint: The client name ends in ctl, meaning control.
hints.stronger_hint: Install /opt/suta/artifacts/etcdctl to /usr/local/bin/etcdctl with mode 0755.
hints.solution: Run the displayed command and wait for ETCDCTL_INSTALLED.

steps.title: Install the etcdutl recovery program
steps.why: etcdutl inspects and restores offline etcd data such as snapshots.
steps.command_explanation: install copies the offline recovery utility and gives it executable permissions.
steps.expected: The command returns to the prompt and /usr/local/bin/etcdutl is executable.
steps.hint: This utility is not the running server and does not contact the cluster for normal health checks.

hints.question: Which utility will inspect an offline snapshot later?
hints.hint: Its name ends in utl, meaning utility.
hints.stronger_hint: Install the staged etcdutl file to /usr/local/bin/etcdutl with mode 0755.
hints.solution: Run the displayed command and wait for ETCDUTL_INSTALLED.

steps.title: Create the protected etcd configuration directory
steps.why: Configuration and consensus data need explicit protected locations.
steps.command_explanation: install -d creates a directory; 0700 allows only root; -o and -g set its owner and group.
steps.expected: The command returns without error and /etc/etcd is owned by root with mode 0700.
steps.hint: Create only /etc/etcd in this action; the data directory is next.

hints.question: Who should be able to read the future member private key?
hints.hint: Only root needs access in this lab.
hints.stronger_hint: Use mode 0700 for both directories.
hints.solution: Create /etc/etcd with root ownership and mode 0700.

steps.title: Create the protected etcd consensus-data directory
steps.why: etcd must persist quorum state in a root-only directory that starts empty.
steps.command_explanation: This creates the separate consensus-data directory with root-only access; it does not initialize a member.
steps.expected: The command returns without error and /var/lib/etcd remains empty, root-owned, and mode 0700.
steps.hint: This is the data directory named by --data-dir in the next configuration step.

hints.question: Why separate configuration from consensus data?
hints.hint: They have different lifecycle and recovery responsibilities.
hints.stronger_hint: Create /var/lib/etcd with root ownership and 0700.
hints.solution: Run the registered install -d command and require ETCD_DATA_DIRECTORY_SECURE.

steps.title: Install the role-bound TLS public certificate
steps.why: Peers need this signed public certificate to authenticate the member name and private address.
steps.command_explanation: This copies only the signed public member certificate; mode 0644 is safe because it contains no private key.
steps.expected: The certificate is installed without printing its contents.
steps.hint: A public certificate may be readable; its matching private key may not.

hints.question: Why can this file be 0644?
hints.hint: It contains identity claims and a public key, not the private key.
hints.stronger_hint: Install member.crt as root:root with mode 0644.
hints.solution: Run the registered install command and require ETCD_MEMBER_CERT_INSTALLED.

steps.title: Install the etcd trust anchor
steps.why: The member needs the lab CA certificate to verify certificates presented by clients and peers.
steps.command_explanation: This installs the public CA certificate used as the mutual-TLS trust anchor.
steps.expected: The CA certificate is installed without exposing any private key.
steps.hint: The CA certificate is public; the CA signing key is never placed on a learner server.

hints.question: Which CA material belongs here?
hints.hint: Only the certificate used for verification.
hints.stronger_hint: Install ca.crt as root:root with mode 0644.
hints.solution: Run the registered install command and require ETCD_CA_INSTALLED.

steps.title: Install the role-bound TLS private key
steps.why: Mutual TLS must identify this member without exposing its private key.
steps.command_explanation: The command copies the platform-issued role identity into the protected etcd directory with root-only permissions.
steps.expected: The command returns without displaying key material.
steps.hint: Never use cat on the private key.

hints.question: Which permission prevents other users from reading the key?
hints.hint: The owner needs read and write; everyone else needs no access.
hints.stronger_hint: That numeric mode is 0600.
hints.solution: Install the key with mode 0600, then install the CA and member certificate in their separately guided steps.

steps.title: Configure dcs-1
steps.why: The first member needs a unique name, addresses, peer list, data directory and mutual-TLS rules.
steps.command_explanation: sudo opens the systemd unit with permission to save; vi lets you enter the exact role-resolved configuration supplied for this step.

configuration.body:
[Unit]
Description=SUTA etcd member
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=root
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/etcd --name={{role}} --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd --listen-client-urls=https://{{private_ip}}:2379 --advertise-client-urls=https://{{private_ip}}:2379 --listen-peer-urls=https://{{private_ip}}:2380 --initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://{{private_ip}}:2380 --initial-cluster={{initial_cluster}} --initial-cluster-state=new --initial-cluster-token={{cluster_token}} --client-cert-auth=true --trusted-ca-file=/etc/etcd/ca.crt --cert-file=/etc/etcd/member.crt --key-file=/etc/etcd/member.key --peer-client-cert-auth=true --peer-trusted-ca-file=/etc/etcd/ca.crt --peer-cert-file=/etc/etcd/member.crt --peer-key-file=/etc/etcd/member.key
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
LimitNOFILE=65536

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

steps.expected: vi opens the new etcd.service file; after saving, systemctl can parse the unit.
steps.hint: Use the role-resolved dcs-1 block exactly; do not substitute an address from another role.

hints.question: Which two values must be unique to dcs-1?
hints.hint: Check --name and this node's listen/advertise addresses.
hints.stronger_hint: The initial cluster list is identical on all three members; name and local addresses differ.
hints.solution: Open the file, enter the supplied dcs-1 unit, save with :wq, then run the validator.

hints.solution: Create /etc/etcd with root ownership and mode 0700.

steps.title: Create the protected etcd consensus-data directory
steps.why: etcd must persist quorum state in a root-only directory that starts empty.
steps.command_explanation: This creates the separate consensus-data directory with root-only access; it does not initialize a member.
steps.expected: The command returns without error and /var/lib/etcd remains empty, root-owned, and mode 0700.
steps.hint: This is the data directory named by --data-dir in the next configuration step.

hints.hint: They have different lifecycle and recovery responsibilities.
hints.stronger_hint: Create /var/lib/etcd with root ownership and 0700.
hints.solution: Run the registered install -d command and require ETCD_DATA_DIRECTORY_SECURE.

steps.title: Install the role-bound TLS public certificate
steps.why: Peers need this signed public certificate to authenticate the member name and private address.
steps.command_explanation: This copies only the signed public member certificate; mode 0644 is safe because it contains no private key.
steps.expected: The certificate is installed without printing its contents.
steps.hint: A public certificate may be readable; its matching private key may not.

hints.question: Why can this file be 0644?
hints.hint: It contains identity claims and a public key, not the private key.
hints.stronger_hint: Install member.crt as root:root with mode 0644.
hints.solution: Run the registered install command and require ETCD_MEMBER_CERT_INSTALLED.

steps.title: Install the etcd trust anchor
steps.why: The member needs the lab CA certificate to verify certificates presented by clients and peers.
steps.command_explanation: This installs the public CA certificate used as the mutual-TLS trust anchor.
steps.expected: The CA certificate is installed without exposing any private key.
steps.hint: The CA certificate is public; the CA signing key is never placed on a learner server.

hints.question: Which CA material belongs here?
hints.hint: Only the certificate used for verification.
hints.stronger_hint: Install ca.crt as root:root with mode 0644.
hints.solution: Run the registered install command and require ETCD_CA_INSTALLED.

steps.title: Install the role-bound TLS private key
steps.why: Mutual TLS must identify this member without exposing its private key.
steps.command_explanation: The command copies the platform-issued role identity into the protected etcd directory with root-only permissions.
steps.expected: The command returns without displaying key material.
steps.hint: Never use cat on the private key.

hints.question: Which permission prevents other users from reading the key?
hints.hint: The owner needs read and write; everyone else needs no access.
hints.stronger_hint: That numeric mode is 0600.
hints.solution: Install the key with mode 0600, then install the CA and member certificate in their separately guided steps.

steps.title: Configure dcs-3
steps.why: The third voting member completes the odd-sized quorum design.
steps.command_explanation: Create the dcs-3 unit using the exact role-resolved configuration supplied for this step.

[Unit]
Description=SUTA etcd member
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
User=root
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/etcd --name={{role}} --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd --listen-client-urls=https://{{private_ip}}:2379 --advertise-client-urls=https://{{private_ip}}:2379 --listen-peer-urls=https://{{private_ip}}:2380 --initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://{{private_ip}}:2380 --initial-cluster={{initial_cluster}} --initial-cluster-state=new --initial-cluster-token={{cluster_token}} --client-cert-auth=true --trusted-ca-file=/etc/etcd/ca.crt --cert-file=/etc/etcd/member.crt --key-file=/etc/etcd/member.key --peer-client-cert-auth=true --peer-trusted-ca-file=/etc/etcd/ca.crt --peer-cert-file=/etc/etcd/member.crt --peer-key-file=/etc/etcd/member.key
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
LimitNOFILE=65536

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

steps.title: Configure Patroni on pg-ha-1
steps.why: The first Patroni member defines the cluster scope, DCS transport, bootstrap rules and local PostgreSQL identity.
steps.command_explanation: Enter the role-resolved pg-ha-1 YAML supplied for this step. Secret tokens are inserted through the protected field and are never rendered into chat.

configuration.body:
scope: {{cluster_scope}}
namespace: /service/
name: {{role}}
restapi:
  listen: {{private_ip}}:8008
  connect_address: {{private_ip}}:8008
etcd3:
  hosts: {{etcd_hosts}}
  protocol: https
  cacert: /etc/patroni/etcd-ca.crt
  cert: /etc/patroni/etcd-client.crt
  key: /etc/patroni/etcd-client.key
bootstrap:
  dcs:
    ttl: 30
    loop_wait: 10
    retry_timeout: 10
    maximum_lag_on_failover: 1048576
    postgresql:
      use_pg_rewind: true
      use_slots: true
      parameters:
        wal_level: replica
        hot_standby: 'on'
        max_wal_senders: 10
        max_replication_slots: 10
  initdb:
    - encoding: UTF8
    - data-checksums
  pg_hba:
{{pg_hba_exact_nodes}}
postgresql:
  listen: {{private_ip}}:5432
  connect_address: {{private_ip}}:5432
  data_dir: /opt/pgsql/data
  bin_dir: /opt/pgsql/bin
  pgpass: /etc/patroni/pgpass
  authentication:
    superuser:
      username: postgres
      password: {{secret:postgres_superuser}}
    replication:
      username: replicator
      password: {{secret:replication}}
  parameters:
    unix_socket_directories: /var/run/postgresql
    password_encryption: scram-sha-256
  create_replica_methods:
    - basebackup
  basebackup:
    checkpoint: fast
tags:
  nofailover: false
  noloadbalance: false
  clonefrom: false

steps.expected: The saved configuration passes YAML, secret-permission and Patroni contract validation.
steps.hint: bootstrap.dcs applies only when the cluster is first initialized.

hints.hint: Find scope and name near the top.

hints.solution: Enter the supplied pg-ha-1 configuration and save; the validator checks structure without exposing passwords.
